prompt: The no_std Rust crate in the lesson compiled to a working 794-byte wasm32-unknown-unknown module with zero Wasm-specific dependencies. Why did that work?
choices: wasm32-unknown-unknown is a built-in rustc compilation target, and crate-type = ["cdylib"] is enough for rustc to emit a .wasm binary directly from a plain extern "C" export
rustc automatically vendors a hidden copy of wasm-bindgen whenever it detects a wasm32 target
Cargo rewrites extern "C" functions into JavaScript source code at compile time
The #![no_std] attribute is what makes a crate wasm-compatible; without it no Rust program can target wasm32

prompt: In the wasm-bindgen-generated JS glue shown in the lesson, what do getArrayU8FromWasm0 and __wbindgen_free actually do?
choices: They build a JS typed-array view over a pointer+length region of the Wasm module's shared linear memory, then free that region on the Rust side -- manual marshalling over shared bytes, not message serialization
They open a network connection back to the Rust compiler to request additional heap memory at runtime
They transpile the Wasm module into asm.js for browsers that lack WebAssembly support
They implement React Native's bridge protocol so React Native apps can call Wasm modules directly

prompt: The Node.js benchmark showed only a roughly 1% gap between the compiled Wasm kernel and the hand-written pure-JS equivalent. What explanation does the lesson give for that small gap?
choices: V8's TurboFan JIT already compiles this kind of tight, monomorphic, pure-double-arithmetic loop close to native speed, so there wasn't a large gap for Wasm to close on this specific workload
WebAssembly.instantiate silently falls back to interpreting JS instead of real Wasm bytecode whenever it runs under Node instead of a browser
The benchmark is invalid because Node.js does not implement the WebAssembly API
Rust's release profile disables all optimizations by default, so the Wasm binary was effectively unoptimized

prompt: With no --dir or --env flags granted, the WASI demo failed to read /etc/hostname with "No such file or directory," even though cat /etc/hostname on the host confirmed the file genuinely exists. What does this show about WASI?
choices: WASI grants no ambient filesystem authority at all -- a path outside an explicitly preopened directory doesn't exist from the module's point of view, not merely "exists but access is denied"
WASI reimplements POSIX permission bits, so the failure means the Wasm module's user ID lacked read permission on /etc/hostname
Wasmtime maintains a hardcoded blocklist of specific system files, including /etc/hostname, that it always hides from guests
The failure proves the wasm32-wasip1 target cannot perform any file I/O under any circumstances

prompt: After granting --dir /tmp/sandboxdir::/sandbox, the program could read /sandbox/greeting.txt but still failed to read /etc/hostname in that same run. What does that specific result demonstrate about WASI's capability model?
choices: A granted capability is scoped to exactly the subtree it names; holding one directory capability grants no broader or ambient access elsewhere, even within the same process invocation
Wasmtime capabilities expire after the first successful file read, so any second read in the same run always fails regardless of path
--dir grants access to the entire host filesystem by default unless a separate --deny flag is also passed
The /etc/hostname read failed only because its host-side file permissions differed from /tmp/sandboxdir/greeting.txt's permissions

prompt: Running wasm-opt -Oz on the wasm-bindgen-built binary took it from 9487 bytes to 7865 bytes. What did that step actually do?
choices: It ran a separate, post-compilation binary-to-binary optimization pass (dead-code elimination, instruction-level size reduction) directly on the .wasm module, independent of the Rust compiler that produced it
It recompiled the original Rust source code from scratch at a different optimization level
It stripped out the WASI imports, converting a wasip1 binary into a wasm32-unknown-unknown one
It minified the generated JavaScript glue file rather than the .wasm binary itself

prompt: What is the key difference between building for wasm32-unknown-unknown versus wasm32-wasip1, per the lesson?
choices: wasm32-unknown-unknown assumes no host interface at all, so the embedder (JS) must supply whatever imports it needs, while wasm32-wasip1 links against a standardized set of OS-like imports (files, clock, env, args) that a standalone runtime like Wasmtime implements directly
wasm32-wasip1 produces a binary format incompatible with the WebAssembly spec that browsers implement
wasm32-unknown-unknown can only return 32-bit integers and cannot produce floating-point results
wasm32-wasip1 is required for every Wasm module, including ones that will only ever run in a browser tab

prompt: Per the lesson's explicit contrast with Tier 3's React Native/Flutter architecture module, what makes Wasm's cross-platform model fundamentally different from both the bridge/JSI approach and the Skia/Impeller rendering approach?
choices: Wasm isn't a UI framework bridging to a native rendering layer -- it's a portable compilation target where the identical compiled bytes run unmodified under any conforming engine, because the spec defines the instruction set and sandbox rather than a per-OS native ABI
Wasm replaces JSI and platform channels with an even faster JSON-based message bridge
Wasm only exists inside React Native's New Architecture and has no standalone runtime outside of it
Flutter and React Native both compile internally to WebAssembly, so Wasm is simply their shared internal format
